title: Two rental townhouse developments move forward
subtitle: Missing middle rentals at Cotton Grass Street and Morrison Road, with debate on density, trees, sidewalks and noise.
overview: The Planning and Strategic Initiatives Committee considered two public hearing items, each proposing 32 stacked townhouse rental units. It recommended both to Council, and each recommendation passed {{vote:m1}} and {{vote:m2}}.

At 265 Cotton Grass Street in the Williamsburg Town Centre, the committee recommended changing commercial land to allow a standalone residential building. The official plan amendment would go to the Region of Waterloo for approval. The units would be market-rate two and three bedroom rentals near shops, a park and transit.

At 7 Morrison Road, the committee recommended an official plan amendment and zoning changes to permit a higher floor space ratio, a greater height and a reduced rear setback. The higher figures reflect the sloped site. The committee also recommended adopting an urban design brief to guide site plan approval.
Council will make the final decisions on both. For residents, the items would add rental housing in two established neighbourhoods.

decisions.item: 265 Cotton Grass Street official plan amendment
decisions.detail: The committee recommended adopting the official plan amendment for Schlegel Urban Developments and forwarding it to the Region of Waterloo for approval.
The committee recommended approving the zoning by-law amendment to allow a standalone multiple dwelling on the former commercial parcel.
The committee recommended adopting the amendment for Klondike Homes and forwarding it to the Region of Waterloo for approval.
The committee recommended approving the zoning by-law amendment for the Klondike Homes proposal.
The committee recommended adopting the urban design brief and directing staff to apply it through site plan approval.

debate: On Cotton Grass Street, one councillor asked about affordability. The applicant said programs for affordable housing work less well on a project this size, so the units would be market rent.

Several councillors pressed on density. One said the committee should keep asking developers for more density and less parking, citing the city's housing pledge. The applicant said the building's height was kept in view of the planned Main Street character. It said it may seek more density on nearby lands closer to Fischer Hallman Road.
On sustainability, a councillor urged the applicant to go beyond the 2015 building code standard. The applicant said the building uses heat pumps and benchmarks well above that standard.

On Morrison Road, a councillor asked about mature trees at the back of the lot. The consultant said the northern setback was widened from about 4.5 metres to preserve more trees, and tree removal would be addressed through site plan and city tree policies.

Councillors also asked about rail noise and sidewalks. A noise and vibration study has been reviewed by the Region. Staff said a sidewalk would be built along the property's frontage and extended as neighbouring lands develop.
